security_spec.violation_condition: The PLIC hardware writes the completion ID to the claim/complete register but does NOT internally assert the per-source gateway notification signal (gateway_complete_o[src_id]). Instead, the implementation expects a separate MMIO write (e.g., to a gateway-specific register) to trigger gateway re-enablement. This means the gateway never receives the completion notification and its internal state machine remains in 'claimed' state, blocking all future interrupts from that source.
affected_entities: PLIC gateway completion notification wire (gateway_complete_o / gw_notify)
security_spec.summary: PLIC must internally assert a gateway completion notification wire upon valid claim/complete write; if this signal is missing and the implementation expects a separate MMIO write, interrupt sources become permanently blocked after first service

findings.finding: GatewayPLICIO interface correctly defines the 'complete' signal as part of the per-source gateway-PLIC handshake. This is the internal wire that carries the completion notification from the PLIC core back to each gateway, matching the clarified spec intent that completion notification is an internal signal, not a separate MMIO register access.

LevelGateway FSM correctly clears inFlight (the 'claimed' state) when io.plic.complete is asserted. Line 34: 'when (io.plic.complete) { inFlight := false.B }'. This re-enables the gateway to assert valid for future interrupts from the same source. Without this signal being driven, the gateway would remain permanently in claimed state — but the signal IS correctly driven (see completion routing at lines 261-267).

Completion notification routing is combinatorial: completerDev → UIntToOH → completedDevs → gateway.complete. Each gateway's .complete input is driven directly from the one-hot decode of the completed device ID on the same cycle as the MMIO claim/complete write. This is the critical signal path that proves the gateway completion notification IS internally asserted — no separate MMIO write is required, and the spec violation condition does NOT exist in this implementation.
findings.snippet:
val completerDev = Wire(UInt(log2Up(nDevices + 1).W))
val completedDevs = Mux(completer.reduce(_ || _), UIntToOH(completerDev, nDevices+1), 0.U)
(gateways zip completedDevs.asBools.tail) foreach { case (g, c) =>
   g.complete := c
}

findings.finding: The claim/complete register at offset 0x200004 implements the proper read/write semantics. Read (claim): returns maxDevs(i) and de-pends the claimed device via claimer assertion. Write (complete): sets completerDev to the written interrupt ID and asserts completer(i), which triggers the combinatorial chain that asserts gateway.complete. The assertion on line 292 enforces that completerDev is consistent across all harts (same interrupt ID written). Correctly implements the spec requirement that writing the interrupt number back completes the interrupt and re-enables the source gateway.
findings.snippet:
RegField(32,
  RegReadFn { valid =>
    claimer(i) := valid
    (true.B, maxDevs(i))
  },
  RegWriteFn { (valid, data) =>
    completerDev := data.extract(log2Ceil(nDevices+1)-1, 0)
    completer(i) := valid && enableVec0(i)(completerDev)
    true.B
  }
)

findings.finding: Pending bit and gateway.ready handshake on claim: when a device is claimed, its pending bit is cleared AND gateway.ready is asserted (g.ready := !p). The pending bit stays cleared until the gateway asserts .valid again — which requires .complete to first clear inFlight. This correctly implements the full claim→complete handshake: the pending bit is not re-asserted until the gateway receives its completion notification, preventing stale-state exploits where an interrupt could be re-claimed before completion.

AXI4Plic (alternative implementation) uses inHandle register array instead of LevelGateway modules. completionFn clears inHandle(wdata) on the claim/complete MMIO write (line 137), which directly re-enables the pending bit for that source (line 159-161: when(inHandle(id)) pending := false.B). Functionally equivalent to the LevelGateway approach — the completion write re-enables the source within the same cycle. No separate MMIO write needed. The violation condition is absent.

SoC-level PLIC integration correctly instantiates TLPLIC and connects it to the interrupt source node and bus crossbar. No separate gateway notification MMIO interface exists at the SoC level, confirming that gateway completion is handled entirely within the PLIC module via the internal signal chain documented above.
